The Concert of Europe was a system of collective great-power diplomacy established after the Napoleonic Wars in 1815. Britain, Russia, Austria, France, and Prussia agreed to manage European affairs through periodic conferences rather than unilateral action. Built on principles of balance-of-power and shared interest in stability, this Concert emerged from the Congress of Vienna, where the victorious powers reorganized Europe after Napoleon's defeat. Metternich, the Austrian foreign minister, was its principal architect and ideologue. He used it to isolate revolutionary movements and preserve autocratic monarchy. The system was based on a principle that major powers should consult before unilateral action, and that the stability of one great power benefits all—a forerunner of modern multilateralism. The Concert intervened collectively in Spain in 1823, recognized Greek independence in 1829, and acted in the Balkans, overriding national sovereignty. It preserved balance-of-power by preventing any single nation from dominating Europe, though this diplomatic mechanism restrained but did not prevent future wars and conflicts. The Concert also suppressed liberal nationalism, opposing Italian unification and Greek independence initially, viewing them as threats to conservative order. Formally lasting until the 1870s, it gradually dissolved as nationalist ambitions and industrial rivalry fractured the post-Napoleonic consensus. After the Crimean War and German unification, rising nationalism and intense industrial competition undermined the consensual foundations the Concert had relied on.
